newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Coles shareholders upset despite brighter outlook.
newsitem.headline: Coles shareholders upset despite brighter outlook.

text.p: Australia's biggest retailer, Coles Myer Ltd, forecast improved profits at its annual meeting on Tuesday but failed to quell dissent from shareholders angry at director dealings and the company's recent under-performance.

"First quarter performance is running above expectations and we hope that can continue," chairman Nobby Clark told the annual meeting in Sydney, adding that provided Christmas trading was reasonable, Coles bottom line results should improve in 1996/97. Clark was jeered during the marathon six-hour meeting when he cut short debate on the re-election to the board of Solomon Lew, whose related-party transactions and connection with the so-called Yannon affair have angered small shareholders.
Lew, who owns about 14 percent of Coles Myer, was eventually re-elected as a director with the help of proxy votes after the floor of the meeting overwhelmingly rejected his re-election.

Coles Myer's net profit fell in the year to July 28, 1996 to A$280.4 million (US$221.5 million) from A$423.4 million a year earlier in a difficult retail environment and continued losses from its toy store chain, World 4 Kids.
Clark repeated that Coles was cutting back the number of standalone World 4 Kids stores to six or seven from 23, but said the brand would be used in Coles' K-Mart and Grace Bros stores.
"There will be a continuing loss from World 4 Kids," he said, adding that the company would be doing everything it could to ensure losses were not significant.
"We made a loss of about A$8 million on the EBIT side in the first quarter," he said. World 4 Kids made a A$35.8 million loss before interest and tax in 1995/96.
Coles initiated its ill-fated World 4 Kids venture in 1994 in response to the entry into the Australian market of the world's largest toy retailer Toys "R" Us Inc.
Clark spent much of the meeting defending Lew, the company's former deputy chairman, fielding questions about a controversial deal known as the Yannon transaction.

Yannon was a financial transaction which cost Coles A$18 million and benefited a company associated Lew by a similar sum. The deal was at the centre of a dispute between the company and sacked finance director, Philip Bowman.
The furore over Bowman's sacking eventually led to Lew's demotion from the position of executive chairman.

Lew mainly holds his stake in Coles through his controlling stake in a company called Premier Investments Ltd. In August, Coles settled the dispute with Lew and Premier over the 1990 Yannon transaction, receiving A$12 million in compensation.

Clark was forced at several points in the meeting to remind shareholders of the defamation laws. After a 1/1-2 hour debate on the motion to re-elect Lew, Clark cut short the debate in the face of loud jeers from the floor.
"You can shout as much as you want, but you will not be heard," he said at one stage as some shareholders tried to reopen the debate.
Lew was re-elected thanks to proxy votes representing 409 million shares, with 83 million shares voting against him.
The discussion about Lew continued to raised in the following 4-1/2 hours of debate over the election of six other directors and the final accounts.
